title: Not money, fame, pleasure or power (ST I-II.2)
hook: Thomas tests each and none can satisfy

segments.voice: Yesterday, mind and will: the mind sees the good, the will loves and chooses it, and the will can't help wanting happiness. Your line was know, then love. Did you do the good you already knew about? Day one thousand one hundred sixty-six.

There's a voice that says it: just one more. One more raise, and then the money will feel like enough. One more round of applause, and then you'll feel like you matter. One more weekend away, one more title on the door, one more good meal, and then, finally, you'll be able to rest. Then the raise comes, and the bar quietly moves. Yesterday Thomas said the will can't help wanting happiness. Fine. But happiness where? The next part of the Summa does something almost like a lab test. Thomas lines up the usual candidates, one at a time, and checks each one. Today: not money.
screen: `JUST ONE MORE.` → `THE BAR QUIETLY MOVES.` → `THOMAS TESTS THE CANDIDATES.`

segments.voice: Money goes first. Thomas notes that money is always for something else: food, a roof, the things it buys. Anything you want only as a means can't be the end you're looking for. Next, honor and fame. Honor, he says, is given to someone because of a good they already have, so it's a sign of the good, not the good itself. And fame lives in other people's heads, where it can be wrong, and can be gone by morning. Then power. Power can be used well or terribly. Anything that can be used for evil can't be the highest good, which by definition no one could misuse. Then pleasure. Thomas doesn't sneer at it. He says pleasure is real, and good, but it follows something good, the way a glow follows a fire. Chase the glow by itself and you lose the fire. Then the big turn. Why does every candidate fail? Not because these things are bad. Thomas calls them goods. They fail because they're limited, and the will is made for the good without limit. Every created good is a part. The will wants the whole. So the hunger outruns every thing we feed it. Jesus puts the question sharply, in the Douay-Rheims: "For what doth it profit a man, if he gain the whole world, and suffer the loss of his own soul?" And he names the mechanism: "For where thy treasure is, there is thy heart also." Thomas's conclusion is that only God can fill it. Tomorrow, he says what that would look like. Today, just the sorting: good things, real things. Not the thing.
screen: `MONEY IS ALWAYS FOR SOMETHING ELSE.` · `HONOR AND FAME ARE SIGNS.` · `POWER CAN BE MISUSED; PLEASURE FOLLOWS.` · `EACH GOOD IS A PART; THE WILL WANTS THE WHOLE.` · then, large: `WHERE THY TREASURE IS, THERE IS THY HEART.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice what you chase. Settle, and breathe. Look back over the last few days with a light touch, no judgment. Where did your attention keep running? Checking the account balance. Refreshing for likes. Planning the next treat. Wanting the last word in an argument. Name one, plainly. Then ask Thomas's question of it: is this for something else? And if I got all of it, would I stop wanting? Don't throw it away. Just set it down in its proper size, a good thing, not the whole thing. If you pray, you can hand that chase to God for a minute. The bell holds the time.
Not money. Thomas tests money, fame, power and pleasure, and finds each a real good that can't be the whole of happiness. Today's word.
Your line: none of these. Today, when you catch yourself saying just one more, name what you're really hoping it will give you. Day one thousand one hundred sixty-six.

howItsDone: Catholic teaching, following Thomas, holds that riches, honor, power and pleasure are real goods but cannot by themselves make a person happy, and this sorting appears in retreats, homilies and teaching on the beatitudes.

he calls them real goods. they fail as happiness because they're limited, and the will wants the good without limit.

like a glow following a fire. chase the glow alone and you lose the fire.

power can be used well or badly. because it can be misused, it can't be the highest good.

fork.setup: you're Thomas, testing fame as the answer to happiness. what's the problem with it?
options: fame lives in other people's heads, where it can be wrong and can vanish.
fame is the answer; the test passes.
fork.reveal: Thomas says fame depends on what others know of you, which can be mistaken and passing. it can't be the lasting good the will wants.

original.note: Latin, the language Thomas wrote in: happiness, blessedness — what Thomas is testing each candidate against.

trapdoor: what you thought: religion says money and pleasure are bad.
what it means: Thomas calls them goods but shows that none of them, alone, can be the whole of happiness.
what a scholar hears: Thomas's reason is that the will's object is the universal good, and no created good is universal.

notes: All Aquinas is paraphrased. Check: wealth sought for something else (I-II.2.1); honor as given on account of an excellence (I-II.2.2); glory/fame depends on human knowledge, which can fail (I-II.2.3); power can be used for good or evil (I-II.2.4); pleasure as a proper accident following the good (I-II.2.6); no created good satisfies because the will's object is the universal good (I-II.2.8). The script skips Thomas's tests of bodily goods and goods of the soul for length.
The 'glow following a fire' image is the script's own, not Thomas's wording.
Douay-Rheims wording to confirm: Matthew 16:26 and Matthew 6:21.
The large screen line shortens Matthew 6:21 for display ('WHERE THY TREASURE IS, THERE IS THY HEART'); the voice quotes it in full.
Editor: the hook's inner voice is now framed as 'a voice that says it' rather than telling the listener what they feel.
